text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended sharply lower following a sharp retracement in New York's arabica futures which came under pressure from speculative and trade selling. Brazil's coffee belt was also expected to escape a damaging cold this weekend although temperatures might drop to below normal levels, weathermen said. July lost $178 per tonne to close at $1,905 per tonne, while September gave up $185 to close at $1,930 per tonne.

Arabica futures in New York tumbled for the second straight session pressured by speculative and trade selling amid an easing of nearby supply concerns. July slid 21.05 cents/lb to close at 230.50 cents/lb, while September lost 15.70 cents/lb to close at 209.40 cents/lb. There has been apparently a change in sentiment following heavy shipments by producers as shown by the latest ICO export data, released Thursday and greater use of cheaper priced Brazilians and robustas.

There is also talk of some coffee being moved from Europe to the United States to satisfy needs. With the differentials now down, more coffee might come to the board to take advantage of the high premium on the spot contract, whereas before there was little incentive to deliver coffee when outrageous premiums could be fetched on top of the futures price, traders said. While supply worries may be alleviated in the short-term, some believe they may re-emerge later this summer ahead of many Latin American countries' autumn harvest.

MEXICO - Mexican coffee roasters, struggling to get their hands on beans from the national crop, have persuaded the government to allow robusta imports this year of 150,000 60-kg bags, industry sources said. Coffee shipments were so heavy this year, spurred in part by attractive prices, that little coffee remains in the country until the new crop starts in October. Mexico exported 3.71 million 60-kg bags in October/April 1996/97, up from 3.47 million bags the previous year. Total production in 1996/97 is forecast at 5.10 million bags, down from 5.37 million bags harvested the previous year.

COSTA RICA - Coffee production in 1996/97 (October/September) is estimated at 3.2 million 60-kg bags, up from nearly 3 million bags the previous year, industry sources said. It was added that if prices continue to be high, production would rise further to 3.5 million bags over the next few years.

UNITED KINGDOM - The UK imported 233,778 bags of coffee in February 1997, 0.5 percent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1997 up to 515,600 bags, 5.6 percent more than was imported the same period in 1996. Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by nearly 12 percent to 3.114 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/February 1997 were Colombia (50,700 vs 42,800 bags), Indonesia (56,900 vs 37,100 bags) and Vietnam (62,100 vs 63,000 bags).
The country exported 76,600 bags of coffee in January/February 1997, 8 percent less than was exported the same period in 1996. Total exports in calendar year 1996 rose by 0.8 percent to 542,600 bags.
